## The data

- [**NHANES**](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/index.htm) stands for the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
- Series of studies designed to assess the health and nutritional status of adults and children in the United States.
- Conducted by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), part of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

## How NHANES Works

- NHANES combines interviews and physical examinations.
- The interview includes demographic, socioeconomic, dietary, and health-related questions.
- The examination part includes medical, dental, and physiological measurements, as well as laboratory tests administered by medical personnel.
- NHANES data is collected in 2-year cycles and released in public-use data files.

## Depression Screening in NHANES
- NHANES includes a depression screening questionnaire known as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9).
- The PHQ-9 consists of 9 questions that assess the frequency of depressive symptoms over the past two weeks.
- Each question is scored from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), resulting in a total score ranging from 0 to 27.

## Cross-sectional data
`nhanes_dpq` contains data from multiple NHANES cycles, including demographic information and responses to the depression questionnaire.
```{webr}
nhanes_dpq
```

## Calculating depression scores
- [PHQ-9](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2021/DataFiles/DPQ_L.htm) is a widely used tool for monitoring and measuring the severity of depression.
- It consists of nine questions that assess the frequency of depressive symptoms over the past two weeks.
- Each question is scored from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), resulting in a total score ranging from 0 to 27.
- A common threshold for indicating depression is a score of 10 or higher.

## PHQ-9 in NHANES
```{r}
nhanes_dpq |> select(starts_with("DPQ"))
```

## Constructing PHQ-9
```{webr}
dep2score <- function(x) {
  case_match(as.integer(x),
    1 ~ 0,
    2 ~ 1,
    3 ~ 2,
    4 ~ 3,
    .default = NA_integer_
  )
}
```

## Operating across rows: `rowwise()`
We'll use new dplyr verbs, `across` and `rowwise()`, to operate across rows.

```{webr}
nhanes_dpq |> sample_n(1000) |>
  filter(!is.na(DPQ010)) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("DPQ"), dep2score)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(DepScore = sum(c_across(DPQ010:DPQ090), na.rm=TRUE),
         Depressed = DepScore >= 10) |>
  ungroup()
```

## Trends in depression over time
```{webr}
nhanes_dpq1 |> 
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(SDDSRVYR, "\\d+"))) |> 
  group_by(year, RIDAGEYR) |> 
  summarise(mean_dep = weighted.mean(DepScore, WTINT2YR, na.rm=TRUE), n=n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=mean_dep, color=as.factor(RIDAGEYR))) + geom_line()
```

##
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
nhanes_dpq1 |> 
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(SDDSRVYR, "\\d+"))) |> 
  group_by(year, RIDAGEYR) |> 
  summarise(mean_dep = weighted.mean(DepScore, WTINT2YR, na.rm=TRUE), n=n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=mean_dep, color=as.factor(RIDAGEYR))) + geom_line() +
  labs(x="Year", y="Mean Depression Score", color="Age") +
  ggtitle("Trends in Depression Scores Over Time by Age Group")
```

## Grouping a factor

```{webr}
(p <- nhanes_dpq1 |> 
  mutate(year = as.integer(str_extract(SDDSRVYR, "\\d+")),
         age_grp = cut(RIDAGEYR, 
                       breaks = c(-1, 17, 30, 45, 60, 120), 
                       labels = c("0-17", "18-29", "30-44", "45-59", "60+"))) |> 
  group_by(year, age_grp) |> 
  summarise(mean_dep = weighted.mean(DepScore, WTINT2YR, na.rm=TRUE), n=n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=year, y=mean_dep, color=age_grp)) + geom_line())
```

## Youth suicide
[WISQARS](https://wisqars.cdc.gov/reports/?o=MORT&y1=2001&y2=2023&t=0&i=2&m=20810&g=00&me=0&s=0&r=0&ry=0&e=0&yp=65&a=5Yr&g1=10&g2=25&a1=0&a2=199&r1=YEAR&r2=AGEGP&r3=NONE&r4=NONE) (Web-based Injury Statistics Query and Reporting System) from the CDC provides data on 
injury-related deaths, including suicides, in the United States.
```{webr}
suicide
```

## Rates of suicide over time
```{webr}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
(p <- ggplot(suicide) + 
  geom_line(aes(x = as.integer(Year), y = `Crude Rate`, color = `Age Group`)))
```

## 
How much did suicide rates increase from 2010-2020?
```{webr}
suicide |> filter(Year %in% c("2010", "2020", "2023")) |> 
  select(`Age Group`, `Year`, `Crude Rate`) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from=Year, values_from=`Crude Rate`) |>
  mutate(percent_inc = `2020` / `2010` * 100 - 100) ->
  pct_inc
```

## Annotate the plot to make it more impactful
```{webr}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
p + geom_text(data=pct_inc, 
  aes(y=`2023`, color=`Age Group`, label=paste0("+", round(percent_inc, 2), "%")),
  x=2024.2) + xlim(c(2000, 2025))
```

# Why are rates of suicide and depression increasing, especially amongst the young?

## Correlation and causation
- We all know what "$X$ is correlated with $Y$" means.
- What does "$X$ causes $Y$" mean?

## Causality in statistics
- Causality means that changes in one variable (the cause) directly lead to changes in another variable (the effect).
- Examples: 
  - "standing in the rain" causes "getting wet"
  - "jogging" causes "increased heart rate"
  
## Non-examples
- "drinking red wine" ~~causes~~ [may be correlated with](https://www.heart.org/en/news/2019/05/24/drinking-red-wine-for-heart-health-read-this-before-you-toast) "less risk of heart disease"
- "Mediterranean diet" ~~causes~~ [is correlated with](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5902736/) "living longer"

## Spurious correlations

[![margarine in Maine](https://www.tylervigen.com/spurious/correlation/image/5920_per-capita-consumption-of-margarine_correlates-with_the-divorce-rate-in-maine.png)](https://www.tylervigen.com/spurious/correlation/5920_per-capita-consumption-of-margarine_correlates-with_the-divorce-rate-in-maine)

## Establishing causality is difficult
- Unlike correlation, which can be directly observed from data, establishing causality is really difficult.
- Let's see an example, again from NHANES.

# Does money cause happiness?
```{webr}
NHANES |> lm(as.integer(Depressed) ~ HHIncomeMid, data=_) |> summary()
```

## Wealthier people sleep more
```{webr}
NHANES |> lm(SleepHrsNight ~ HHIncomeMid, data=_) |> summary()
```

##  Wealthier people are in better shape
```{webr}
NHANES |> lm(BMI ~ HHIncomeMid, data=_) |> summary()
```

## Wealthier people are less likely to smoke
```{webr}
NHANES |> mutate(smoke = Smoke100 == "Yes") |> lm(smoke ~ HHIncomeMid, data=_) |> summary()
```

## The challenge of proving that wealth causes happiness
- When I condition on the wealth level, I'm also conditioning on all the other factors
  that are also correlated with wealth.
- It's impossible to isolate the effect of wealth on happiness from observational data.
- The extra factors that are correlated with both wealth and happiness are called **confounders**.

## Famous example of confounding
In the 1970s UC Berkeley was sued for gender bias in admissions to its graduate programs.
```{webr}
ucb1
```
## Omitted variable bias
- The overall data shows a bias against women.
- But: there is another variable lurking in the background: the choice of department.
- Some departments are more competitive than others.
- Women tend to apply to more competitive departments.

##
```{webr}
UCBAdmissions |> apply(3, prop.test)
```

## Simpson's paradox
(When the trend appears in several different groups of data but disappears or reverses when these groups are combined.)
```{r}
ucbt <- UCBAdmissions |> as_tibble() |> pivot_wider(names_from=Admit, values_from=n)
ucbt |> group_by(Gender) |> summarize(Admitted = sum(Admitted), Rejected = sum(Rejected)) |>
  mutate(Dept = "Overall") |> bind_rows(ucbt) |>
  mutate(admit_rate = Admitted / (Admitted + Rejected)) |>
  ggplot() + geom_line(aes(x=Gender, y=admit_rate, group=Dept, color=Dept))
```
